chapter: Brother Lorenzo Tio Jr. and his career
title: Lorenzo in New York, publishers' tricks and leaving Piron
summary: Lorenzo avoided publicity because New York publishers could copy numbers with small changes; he left Piron to go on his own, bought a home in Mount Vernon, and Piron later regretted not heeding him.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: How about the Red Man Blues? Did he write that? Red Man Blues? I don't know. I don't know.
Bruce Cochard have a record of it if you ever want to hear him. He played a clarinet and a Red Man.

Yeah. I wouldn't know. I know that he played many a number such as, uh, um, I know he had clarinet solo one time in, uh, I wish, at P. Rowe's number. Um, Sister Kate. I wish I knew what it was. Sister Kate. Well, he, uh, he did a lot of numbers, but I don't know what they were because he was in New York and I was here. Of course, he didn't believe in going around a whole lot of publicity. He knew that, uh, New York had a lot of racket to it. And, uh, he knew that if in case he would get, uh, they'd tell you, well, uh, give me your copy now and I'll, I'll look it over and probably, uh, I'll, I'll tell you what it's all about in about two, three weeks or so. Well, of course, they got a chance of taking all your number down, you see. And with a few different arrangements, a few bars that they're different, well, they got your number. You can't get back at them because they, they have your under, they got you.
Yeah, a few little changes and they can still copy right now.

See? Yeah. Well, your original copy when you go to cope with that, this is your copy. This is his copy. Well, they didn't change the bar. You, you, you can't, you can't fight them for that. Well, he made a lot of numbers that I don't know anything about. Yes. But he's got a daughter that's in New York. They, he did pretty well because I know he bought a home in, um, in New York, in Mount Juan in New York.
He stayed up there when he went up to Pierron, did he, and stayed on?

Yeah, he left Pierron. He left, left here and went on up there, he said. And he was going out for yourself. He told Pierron that up in case jazz was getting, be popular down here and they were unable to, they want youngsters that can produce. He said, I can produce. I can play. I want you to get some other fella that can play that hold me up. Well, no, you wanted that particular part of, uh, this way of his band, the way that he wanted it. Well, he said, if y'all want it that way, I'm going to New York. And he left. And Pierron often times told me that I'm sorry that I never did listen to Big Brother, he used to call him. Yeah. He said, he often told me, he said, if I, I should change my, my band. And so, he didn't, so my brother went to New York, he made, he made famous circles.
